name: Genesis Block
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Block Zero: Where a Chain Has No Chain to Point To
lesson.summary: The genesis block is the very first block of a blockchain, unique because it has no previous block to reference, and it is typically hardcoded into a network's software as the trusted starting point every node builds from.
lesson.body:
Every earlier section in this chapter has described a block's header as containing the hash of the block before it, which raises an obvious question about the very first block ever created: what does it point back to, if nothing came before it? The answer is the genesis block, the founding exception to the rule. It is either given a previous block hash field of all zeros, or the field is simply omitted or treated as meaningless, since by definition there is no prior header to hash.

This is not a minor technical footnote, it is the anchor for everything discussed in the block structure and block header sections. If every block's legitimacy rests on correctly referencing the block before it, that chain of references has to bottom out somewhere in a block that is trusted for a different reason entirely: because it is hardcoded directly into the software that node operators download and run. When Bitcoin software starts up for the first time, it does not go looking on the network for block zero, it already contains the genesis block's exact contents built into the program itself, and every other block it accepts must ultimately trace an unbroken hash chain back to that fixed starting point.

This connects back to the block structure discussed earlier: the genesis block typically follows the same header and body format as every other block, just with an empty or symbolic previous hash field and, often, a small number of initial transactions, sometimes just one. Bitcoin's genesis block, mined by Satoshi Nakamoto in January 2009, contains a single transaction with a small reward and a text string embedded in its data: a headline from that day's Times of London newspaper referencing a bank bailout. That text served a real purpose beyond commentary: it proved the block could not have been created before that date, since the headline did not exist yet, giving the genesis block a verifiable timestamp lower bound.

A useful way to think about why the genesis block has to be hardcoded rather than discovered: trust has to start somewhere. A brand new node joining the network cannot verify the entire chain is legitimate purely from cryptography alone, because cryptography can only tell you whether block 500,000 correctly follows block 499,999, all the way back, it cannot tell you whether the very first block in that sequence was the "real" one versus some other party's fabricated alternative history. The genesis block is the one piece of the system where trust is established the old fashioned way, by everyone agreeing in advance, through the software they choose to run, on what block zero actually is.

It is worth being clear eyed about the implication: the entire immutability property discussed earlier in this chapter, the idea that history cannot be rewritten, ultimately rests on this one universally agreed upon starting point. If a community of node operators disagreed badly enough about the network's rules or history, they could, in principle, define a new genesis block and start an entirely separate chain, which is close to what happens during certain contentious network splits. The genesis block is not proof against disagreement, it is simply the shared starting assumption that makes agreement possible in the first place.
